items.t: Northrop Grumman stock links with Hermeus on high-Mach aircraft
sum: Northrop Grumman and Hermeus are joining forces on an uncrewed, high-Mach aircraft program, adding a new development thread to the defense contractor's aerospace portfolio.

On Friday, November 13, 2026, American Machinist reported that Northrop Grumman had reached a strategic teaming agreement with Hermeus. Northrop Grumman is contributing mission systems and autonomy technology, including sensing, communications, navigation and command-and-control capabilities.

The program combines Northrop Grumman's experience integrating operational technology onto aircraft with Hermeus' rapid development model. The effort is tied to a 219-million-US-dollar contract from the US Defense Innovation Unit, while flight tests are scheduled to continue through 2027.

For investors, the agreement provides another example of Northrop Grumman positioning its electronic warfare, communications, sensing and autonomy capabilities for emerging military programs. The commercial effect will depend on development progress, contract execution and future procurement decisions.

On Wednesday, November 11, Northrop Grumman was scheduled to participate in the Baird 2026 Global Industrial Conference. In its conference announcement, the company said Chair, Chief Executive Officer and President Kathy Warden would present at 10:40 a.m. Eastern time. The appearance put management's operating priorities and investment plans in focus during the week.

Northrop Grumman stock sees stronger international growth path
sum: Northrop Grumman CEO Kathy Warden presented a stronger long-term growth case at the Baird Global Industrial Conference on Wednesday, November 11, 2026. In remarks carried by Investing.com, she pointed to durable demand across the defense contractor's portfolio and an expanding international opportunity.

Northrop Grumman expects sales to grow by 5 percent to 7 percent in 2027, with further momentum into 2028. Warden said the outlook assumes that a continuing federal funding resolution will extend into early 2027, allowing key programs to continue without major disruption.

International sales were about 4.3 billion US dollars year to date, and management expects them to exceed 10 billion US dollars by 2031. Warden also highlighted national security space, which now accounts for more than 15 percent of company sales and is benefiting from rising demand for communications, sensing, missile tracking and resilient space systems.

Near-term growth is expected from munitions, counter-drone technology and integrated air and missile defense. The company said products such as IBCS are growing at double-digit rates and should contribute to revenue in 2027. Longer-term opportunities include the B-21 bomber, the Sentinel missile program, microelectronics and quantum computing.

Northrop Grumman plans capital spending of about 4.5 percent of sales in 2027 and 2028 as it expands capacity. Management expects spending to return to about 3 percent of sales after the required capacity is in place, potentially creating a later cash-flow inflection point.

sum: Intuitive Machines, Inc. LUNR is slated to report third-quarter 2026 results on Nov. 12, before market open. The company delivered a negative earnings surprise of 128.57% in the last reported quarter.

In particular, continued execution across satellite manufacturing programs, including the production of satellites for the Space Development Agency's (SDA) Tranche 2 and Tranche 3 tracking layers, is expected to have supported revenues. Additionally, progress on the Near Space Network Services (NSNS) program, ongoing lunar mission activities and the delivery of communication satellites for commercial customers are likely to have contributed to LUNR's third-quarter top-line performance.

Strong revenue generation, along with higher gross profit earned through growing contributions from the satellite manufacturing business and continued focus on cost management and efficient program execution, is likely to have boosted LUNR's third-quarter bottom-line performance.

However, higher selling, general and administrative expenses due to continued investments in infrastructure, increased production capacity, inventory purchases and integration costs related to recent acquisitions are likely to hurt the third-quarter results. Additionally, elevated research and development expenses related to lunar lander upgrades, the expansion of the company's satellite architecture and the development of future communications and navigation services are likely to have weighed on profitability.

Trump’s US$1.5 trillion defence budget request set to be blocked by Democrats
sum: WASHINGTON – The Republicans’ midterm defeat is crushing any remaining hopes that Congress will approve President Donald Trump’s unprecedented US$1.5 trillion (S$1.92 trillion) defence budget request amid an unpopular war in the Middle East.

Democrats, who won solid majorities of both Chambers of Congress on Nov 3, were already largely opposed to the 44% increase from the previous fiscal year and are now signalling that they will block any efforts to push it forward.

At the same time, Republican lawmakers returning to the lame-duck session before the new Congress is seated in January 2027 may not be able to muster the support or political will to ram through the massive defence spending package, especially amid the Pentagon’s unpopular war against Iran that cost many of them their jobs.

“We must push for the development of a more realistic and sustainable approach to our national security – one that does not require a defence budget in excess of US$1 trillion or one paid for with draconian cuts to critical domestic programmes,” Representative Adam Smith of Washington, the incoming chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, said in a statement after the election.

The Democratic resistance risks imperilling some of Trump’s splashiest defence ambitions, including the Golden Dome missile shield and his Trump-class battleship plan, and bodes poorly for defence contractors – some of which also face the prospect of congressional scrutiny over alleged conflicts of interest with the Trump administration.
Shares of major contractors, including Lockheed Martin Corp and Northrop Grumman Corp, fell this week as the midterm results eroded expectations of a ramp-up in US military spending.

Lawmakers returning to Washington on Nov 9 are going to have to grapple with the annual defence policy Bill and a spending plan for fiscal year 2027 – which began on Oct 1 under stopgap funding that runs out on Dec 11.

NASA shares major Moon Base updates at the MAX POWER expo: Here’s what comes next
sum: NASA shares Moon Base updates at the MAX POWER expo, including a nuclear-powered rover and new lander deals

A permanent lunar base will need much more than just astronauts. It will need reliable supply transport, power systems, scouting vehicles, and much more. And to turn this ambitious vision into reality, NASA has announced major updates to its contracts and lunar landers that will fill gaps in its Moon Base program. The details were shared during the agency’s two-day MAX POWER aerospace expo, which is currently being held at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida and will run till November 08, 2026.

More momentum for the Moon Base! NASA has awarded six new launch and in-space transportation task orders to American companies, advancing the capabilities for future missions supporting Moon Base such as CAPSTONE 02, LCRNS, and MoonFall.

As part of its latest update, NASA selected eight companies for the next stage of its Commercial Lunar Payload Services program, known as CLPS. These are the companies that will help build and take payloads from Earth to the surface of the Moon. With this, the first elements of the Moon Base will already be on the surface when astronauts return with Artemis IV. According to the announcement, the selected group is Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, iSpace US, Lockheed Martin Space, Northrop Grumman Space Systems, SpaceX, and Voyager Technologies.

Voyager has been selected for @NASA CLPS 2 contract, making it eligible to compete for future lunar missions through 2036 under a $10 billion base ceiling. The selection expands its role in the Moon Base Program as Griffin-1 prepares for launch to the lunar South Pole. Learn more at https://t.co/POij0YHyii. $VOYG #AcceleratingtheAdvantage #MissionReady

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said, “We are building the Moon Base mission by mission. Today’s announcements expand nearly every part of that campaign, using the playbook that carried NASA through its greatest eras: fly often, learn, apply those lessons, and get more better and more capable with every mission. When our astronauts return to the Moon, they will arrive with the first elements of the Moon Base already waiting for them on the surface.”

sum: The overwhelming victory by the Democrats in the midterm elections shook up Wall Street this week
The biggest tremors were felt in shares of companies tied to the boom in artificial intelligence on concerns that a Democratic Congress will put the brakes on further development of data centers.
Defense and oil companies fell on expectations Democrats would push for an end to the U.S.-Iran war, which would likely lower energy prices.

Meanwhile, hospital shares rose on the possibility that funding for several government programs could be restored or boosted, while liquor companies and others buffeted by tariffs rose on hopes for relief.
Here’s a look at how certain stocks and industries reacted to the result of the midterms.

The frantic construction of data centers to power the AI boom has meant big profits for a wide array of companies — chip makers, power providers, cooling system producers, cloud computing companies and more. Investors hungry for a piece of those profits dove in, pushing some stocks up by double or more. But concerns grew that AI stocks got too pricey. And then the Democrats swept the midterms to take control of Congress.

Nvidia, Lam Research and others tied to the AI boom swung wildly this week on worries that Democratic victories in statehouses across the country could mean a slowdown in further construction, particularly in Texas. Hyperscalers, or those funding the buildout, like Amazon, fared better.

Northrop Grumman stock: Backlog drives higher 2026 profit view
sum: Northrop Grumman reported stronger third-quarter demand on October 20, 2026, and raised its 2026 profit outlook after a surge in contract awards. The company said in its SEC-filed earnings release that third-quarter sales increased 7 percent year over year to 11.122 billion US dollars.

All four operating sectors contributed to the increase. Aeronautics Systems sales advanced 14 percent to 3.575 billion US dollars, while Defense Systems sales climbed 12 percent to 2.307 billion US dollars. Mission Systems and Space Systems each grew sales by 2 percent.

Northrop Grumman secured 16.4 billion US dollars in net awards during the quarter, producing a book-to-bill ratio of 1.5 times. Total backlog reached 109.6 billion US dollars at September 30, including major awards of 2.0 billion US dollars for the Sentinel program, 1.4 billion US dollars for Virginia-class submarines and 1.3 billion US dollars for the F-35 program.

The backlog provides a stronger base for future sales, but execution remains central to the investment case. Aeronautics Systems benefited from higher F-35, B-21 and B-2 sustainment activity, while Defense Systems gained from Sentinel and rocket motor programs. Mission Systems faced lower operating income because a favorable prior-year contract adjustment did not recur.

Net earnings rose 2 percent to 1.124 billion US dollars, while diluted earnings per share increased to 7.89 US dollars from 7.67 US dollars a year earlier. The earnings increase also reflected a lower effective tax rate of 13.4 percent, compared with 16.9 percent in the prior-year quarter. Operating margin narrowed to 11.4 percent from 11.9 percent, making the profit improvement less dependent on sales growth alone.

Northrop Grumman raised its 2026 MTM-adjusted EPS outlook to 29.35 to 29.75 US dollars from 28.60 to 29.10 US dollars. The midpoint increased by 0.70 US dollars. Segment operating income guidance rose to 4.940 billion to 5.040 billion US dollars from 4.850 billion to 5.000 billion US dollars, while sales guidance stayed at 43.750 billion to 44.250 billion US dollars. Adjusted free cash flow guidance remained 3.1 billion to 3.5 billion US dollars.

AI data center stocks dip, renewables surge after Democrat sweep in US midterm elections
sum: Nov 4 (Reuters) – Data center stocks slipped in premarket trading on Wednesday, while clean-energy shares surged after Democrats won both the Senate and the House, raising prospects of tougher oversight of the AI boom alongside fresh backing for renewables.
The Democrats scored sweeping victories in Republican strongholds such as Kansas for the first time in generations.
Texas and Georgia, which are key states for data centers given their ability to host large-scale facilities, also elected Democratic candidates.
The results will usher in a divided government in Washington, following two years in which the Republican-controlled Congress rarely exercised its power to rein in President Donald Trump.
Market reaction spanned sectors including AI-linked stocks, renewables, healthcare companies and prison operators.
Data center operators lost ground, with Core Scientific down 2.8% and Iren down 1.4%. Applied Digital and CoreWeave were marginally lower.

The data center boom triggered public backlash this year, stoking concerns that tighter Democratic oversight could curb spending momentum at a time when investors are becoming wary of mounting AI outlays yet to deliver strong financial returns.

sum: Northrop Grumman (NYSE:NOC) is scheduled to report its earnings on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. The company has a market value of about $73.9 billion. Over the last twelve months it generated around $42 billion in revenue and $4.2 billion in operating profit, with net income of $4.18 billion.

Nobody knows how the market will take the numbers. What we can measure is how Northrop Grumman stock has reacted to its past earnings releases, which is useful context for anyone trading around the event.
Some observations on one-day (1D) post-earnings returns, measured from the last close before each release:
- There are 20 earnings releases in the last five years, with 10 positive and 10 negative one-day (1D) returns. Positive 1D returns were seen 50% of the time.
- The median of the 10 positive 1D returns is 1.9%, and the median of the 10 negative ones is -5.3%.
The table below shows the 1D, 5-day (5D) and 21-day (21D) returns after each release, followed by summary statistics.

Another approach is to wait for the initial reaction and ask whether it tends to continue. The table below shows the correlation between the 1D return and the return over the following 5 and 21 trading days, and between the 5D return and the following 21 trading days. Defense contractors would be barred from buying back their stock in bill approved by Senate panel
sum: The Senate Armed Services Committee approved a must-pass bill with a provision that could bar some defense contractors from executing stock buybacks or paying dividends unless they have Defense Department approval.

The measure, an annual bill known as the National Defense Authorization Act, was approved 18-9 in a closed-door committee meeting last week. The stock buyback provision's inclusion in the committee's bill greatly increases its chances of becoming law and sets up a potential sea change in how the Pentagon interacts with some of the country's largest businesses.

Its bipartisan nature also underscores how Republicans under President Donald Trump have abandoned some of their free-market orthodoxy to join with more interventionist Democrats. The mandate is expected to face fierce blowback from the companies to which it would apply, such as Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman and Boeing.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., a committee member, helped secure the measure's inclusion in the committee's bill. In an interview, she said it's intended to "bring a small amount of discipline to these defense contractors who have been running wild for years."

"These giant defense contractors buy back their own stock for the sole purpose of plumping up the stock price and improving the pay of the corporate executives," she said. "The restriction in the NDAA says if you're a company that's not even performing on your government contracts, you don't get to do that."

The provision in the bill, Section 815, specifically would prohibit the Pentagon from entering into contracts with contractors unless the contractor agrees in writing not to "purchase an equity security of such entity, or any parent entity of such entity, that is listed on a national securities exchange" or "pay dividends or make any other capital distribution with respect to the equity securities of the entity."
The provision would take effect June 15, 2027. The defense secretary could agree to waive the limitation if the contractor provides a "qualifying defense investment plan."

The stock has moved higher primarily because investors are pricing in sustained, multi-year demand for missile defense systems and nuclear modernization programs, which are critical technologies governments are prioritizing to counter evolving threats.

These systems are designed to detect and intercept incoming missiles, while programs like the B-21 stealth bomber support long-range strike capabilities, and both are funded through long-term contracts that provide strong revenue visibility and predictable earnings growth.

At the Citi Global Industrial Tech & Mobility Conference, CEO Kathy Warden said the company is seeing an “unprecedented demand cycle” across global defense markets, with 2026 guidance calling for mid-single-digit revenue growth, segment operating margins in the low to mid-11% range, and free cash flow of $3.1 billion to $3.5 billion, highlighting continued strength across missile defense, space systems, and next-generation platforms.

Analyst and institutional activity further supported the move. Analysts broadly maintained Buy or Overweight ratings with price targets near current levels, while institutional positioning remained active, with Mirabella Financial Services LLP increasing its stake by 148.7% to 5,129 shares worth about $3.1 million and Holocene Advisors opening a new position of 225,300 shares valued at roughly $137.3 million, even as AllianceBernstein reduced its stake by 22.4%.

Compared to competitors like Lockheed Martin, which is more exposed to mature aircraft programs, and RTX, which has greater exposure to commercial aerospace cycles, Northrop Grumman’s heavier focus on newer programs such as the B-21 bomber, missile defense systems, and space platforms positions it earlier in the defense investment cycle, helping explain its stronger stock performance this year.

sum: Global defense stocks jumped on Monday as investors reacted to a dramatic military escalation in the Middle East over the weekend.
The sector was a rare bright spot amid a broader market sell-off triggered by fears of a wider regional conflict.

Germany's Hensoldt and Britain's BAE Systems were among the top performers in the Stoxx 600, up close to 5% and around 6%, respectively. Defense name Renk rose more than 3%, and Leonardo gained more than 2%, paring earlier gains. The broader Stoxx 600 index fell more than 1%, touching a two-week low.
Stateside, U.S. firms Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman rose more than 3% and about 6%, respectively. The S&P 500 traded just above the flatline, rebounding from earlier losses.

With South Korean markets closed Monday, regional activity in Asia-Pacific defense sector was somewhat muted. Japan's defense heavyweights Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and IHI rose roughly 3% each, while Singapore's ST Engineering climbed 2.8%.

The moves come after the U.S. and Israel launched widespread attacks on Iran over the weekend that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, ending his 36-year rule. Retaliatory strikes by Iran against U.S. bases in the Middle East killed three U.S. service members.
Prospects of an escalation also led oil prices and energy companies' shares to surge.

items.t: Northrop Grumman's 2.2 Backlog Coverage: What It Means for Owners
sum: In plain English Northrop Grumman is a capacity business that sells time. Its factories, engineering teams, test ranges, and supply chain exist to deliver long-lived national-security programs over many years. For investors, the key question is therefore not whether any single quarter surprises by 2%3%, but whether Northrop can keep its production system steadily loaded with contracted work while improving execution and cash conversion over time. My thesis is that Northrop's durability and upside are best understood through a single, monitorable number: backlog coverage.

Backlog coverage is total backlog divided by annual sales. It answers a simple question an intelligent investor actually cares about: How many years of revenue are already sold? When backlog coverage rises and stays high, it usually means three things that compound into shareholder returns: revenue becomes less cyclical, margins become more resilient because utilization is steadier, and free cash flow becomes more predictable, enabling consistent dividends and buybacks. Northrop already sits in that attractive zone today, and the multi-year trend suggests the company can continue to monetize strategic modernization programs even as it works through near-term program noise.

Backlog coverage Backlog is the queue of contracted work Northrop is obligated to deliver; sales is the rate at which it burns through that queue. The ratio is therefore years of work on the books. At December 31, 2024, Northrop reported total backlog of $91.468 billion and 2024 sales of about $41.0 billion, implying backlog coverage of roughly 2.2. Put differently, before Northrop signs a single new contract, it already has about two-plus years of revenue under contract.

What makes this KPI more informative than a generic backlog number is that Northrop also discloses backlog quality. At year-end 2024, funded backlog was $39.662 billion and unfunded backlog was $51.806 billion. Funded backlog is the portion backed by appropriated funding (or otherwise committed); unfunded backlog is authorized but not yet fully funded. In practical terms, funded backlog is the money already cleared, while unfunded is authorized demand that still depends on timing and appropriations.

sum: UC aerospace engineering student talks about her internship with Northrop Grumman
The Ohio Federal Research Network highlighted a University of Cincinnati graduate who is now working for Northrop Grumman.

UC College of Engineering and Applied Science graduate Rebecca Gilligan received a bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering and a master's degree in aerospace engineering through UC's Accelerated Engineering Degree program in which students can earn multiple degrees simultaneously.
At UC, Gilligan worked in the UAV Master Lab under Professor Kelly Cohen.
“Rebecca consistently approached research with an engineer’s mindset — focused on validation, robustness and real-world performance,” Cohen told the Ohio Federal Research Network.
The network fosters research collaborations between Ohio universities and industry and government partners on projects in technology, aerospace, defense, energy and health.

Gilligan graduated in 2023. Now she has an internship with aerospace and defense company Northrop Grumman. She told the Ohio Federal Research Network that her work with autonomous systems at UC prepared her to contribute to research and development in industry.

Defeating Drone Threats
sum: Maximizing Battlefield Flexibility with Innovative Guns and Ammunition

On today’s battlefield, the hum of a drone overhead has become all too familiar. Affordable and easy to fly, these unmanned systems are one of the most commonly used tactics by adversaries of the U.S. and allies to gather intelligence, evade traditional defenses and quickly launch precise attacks.

With drone threats advancing faster than ever, Northrop Grumman’s flexible, cutting-edge technology marries speed with innovation to defeat drones like never before. Through close collaboration with our warfighters and partners, we drive continuous innovation — anticipating emerging challenges and providing the precise capabilities needed, exactly when and where they matter most. Building upon the reliability and precision of the Bushmaster family of Chain Guns that our customers know us for, our teams are building next-generation weapon systems and ammunition to elevate battlefield adaptability.

“We built this technology because the need is real — and it’s ready now to help protect those on the front lines,” said Rylan Harris, director of business development for Northrop Grumman armament systems. His team works on the M230LF Dual Feed Bushmaster® Chain Gun, which was engineered to address the growing counter unmanned aircraft systems (C-UAS) threat. “In the end, defeating drones comes down to reliable capability and the Bushmaster Dual Feed with our proximity ammunition will win the fight.”

Currently, warfighters need one type of ammunition to defeat ground threats and another to defeat drones. With the Dual Feed cannon, operators can switch between these two ammunition types with the push of a button, with no time lost reloading or changing weapons. When seconds matter for survival, this mission flexibility gives an instant battlefield advantage.
“Seeing the emerging needs of the warfighter as C-UAS threats evolve, our team moved with urgency,” Rylan said. “We saw where the battlefield was going and built a solution to meet it.”
The versatility of the Dual Feed cannon enables commanders to respond swiftly to both unmanned aircraft systems threats and ground combat situations, adapting to rapidly changing mission demands.

items.t: Northrop Grumman stock rises on $86.1 million contract
sum: Northrop Grumman stock (ISIN US6668071029) is trading around $539.47, down 1.05 percent on September 1, 2026, while a new $86.1 million U.S. Air Force order and a second-quarter beat keep the defense group in view.

According to MarketScreener, Northrop Grumman won an $86.1 million task order for the U.S. Air Force's Remote Visual Assessment program, with $15.2 million obligated immediately and work scheduled through September 2031. The same report says the award was made without competition, which gives the order a clearer strategic profile than a routine small-ticket contract.
Investing.com also reported the award on September 1, 2026, and said the contract is expected to be completed by September 2031.

MarketBeat said Northrop Grumman reported second-quarter EPS of $7.68 and revenue of $10.88 billion, above analyst expectations of $6.82 EPS and $10.80 billion in sales. The company also set FY 2026 guidance at 28.600-29.100 EPS, while sell-side analysts in that report projected 28.97 EPS for the full year.

That is a clean comparison: EPS beat consensus by $0.86, and revenue beat estimates by $80 million. The prior-year comparison in the same report shows $8.15 EPS in the second quarter of 2025, so earnings eased year on year even as the top line moved higher by 5.1 percent.

For investors, the important part is not only the $86.1 million headline but the fact that the work runs through September 2031 and comes with $15.2 million in immediate fiscal 2026 funding. That makes the contract visible in the near-term budget picture, not just in long-cycle backlog language.
Northrop Grumman shares also remain above the 52-week low of $479.02 and below the 52-week high of $774.00, with a market capitalization of $76.67 billion in the latest market snapshot.

Trump says he will not permit dividends and stock buybacks for defense companies
sum: President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he "will not permit" defense companies to issue dividends or stock buybacks until those firms speed up their production of military equipment and address his other complaints about the industry.
Trump, in a lengthy Truth Social post, also took aim at defense contractors' executive pay packages, calling them "exorbitant and unjustifiable."
"Defense Companies are not producing our Great Military Equipment rapidly enough and, once produced, not maintaining it properly or quickly," he wrote.
Until those companies build new production plants, "no Executive should be allowed to make in excess of $5 Million Dollars," Trump declared.
Shares of General Dynamics, Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman each fell about 3% following Trump's comments.

Trump later singled out Raytheon as "the least responsive to the needs of the Department of War, the slowest in increasing their volume, and the most aggressive spending on their Shareholders rather than the needs and demands of the United States Military."

He said that the Pentagon will cut its business ties with Raytheon unless it "steps up" on investment in plants and equipment, adding that "under no circumstances" can the company do any more stock buybacks in the meantime.
